comparison: Both evaluations SUPPORT the main findings for 9-month-olds (C29-C32). OpenEval provides detailed statistical justification (p-values, effect sizes, sample sizes), while peer reviewers affirm these as 'important findings' and 'main findings' that are 'mostly well supported by data.'

Both evaluations SUPPORT the discrepancy with prior work (C33). OpenEval notes it 'warrants discussion but doesn't invalidate the findings,' while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the contradiction with Maister et al. 2017 as noteworthy but valid.

Both address C40-C42 regarding 3-month-old findings. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to inconclusive respiratory results and power concerns, while peer reviewers SUPPORT the findings, accepting the pattern of cardiac replication with inconclusive respiratory evidence as part of the developmental trajectory.

Both evaluations address 18-month null findings (C34-C37). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN emphasizing inadequate sample size and inconclusive equivalence tests, while peer reviewers SUPPORT the findings, accepting them as 'less reliable effects' with acknowledged technical challenges.

Both reference simulation analysis (C39). OpenEval uses simulations as evidence of inadequate power (UNCERTAIN rating), while peer reviewers praise the simulation approach as a strength that helps 'overcome limitations' and provide convincing evidence (SUPPORTED).

Both address cardiac MEGA-analysis findings (C49, C52). OpenEval SUPPORTS with detailed statistical justification, and peer reviewers also SUPPORT, describing 'convincing evidence' and praising the 'extensive statistical analyses.'

Both address respiratory MEGA-analysis findings (C50, C53). OpenEval SUPPORTS but notes weaker evidence than cardiac findings, while peer reviewers also SUPPORT, acknowledging 'less reliable effects' for respiratory data especially at 18 months.

Both address the relationship between cardiac and respiratory interoception (C54-C56, C76). OpenEval SUPPORTS with caution about 18-month sample size, while peer reviewers also SUPPORT, affirming the finding of a relationship at 18 months only as an important developmental pattern.

Both reference contextualization with existing literature (C73). OpenEval includes this in SUPPORTED evaluation of developmental relationships, while peer reviewers accept the finding as consistent with literature regarding no relationship in younger infants.

Both address longitudinal stability findings (C58-C61, C129). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to very small sample (N=19-20) and insufficient power, while peer reviewers SUPPORT, accepting the null longitudinal finding without challenge as part of the study's mixed results.

Both address exploratory cross-sectional developmental findings (C62-C65, C130). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN emphasizing the exploratory nature and contradiction with confirmatory analyses, while peer reviewers SUPPORT, accepting 'preliminary evidence for an increase in respiratory interoception' as a valid exploratory finding.

Both address specification curve analysis (C66-C68, C70). OpenEval SUPPORTS the methodological approach and robustness findings, while peer reviewers also strongly SUPPORT, calling it 'extremely helpful' and providing 'compelling evidence' about analytical choices.

Both address specific analytical decisions identified in specification curve (C92-C96). OpenEval SUPPORTS the transparent documentation of impactful decisions, while peer reviewers also SUPPORT, praising the evidence about how analytical choices explain effects.

Both address the fixed-order design error (C108-C112, C135). OpenEval SUPPORTS the transparent reporting but notes it as a 'serious limitation,' while peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly identifying it as a 'critical weakness' that 'may have critically influenced the results.'

Both address mitigation analyses for the design flaw (C113-C115). OpenEval SUPPORTS the additional analyses as providing 'some reassurance' while acknowledging unresolvable confounds, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the mitigation but maintaining concerns about critical influence.

Both address sample size and attrition (C120-C125). OpenEval SUPPORTS the transparent reporting while noting concerns about generalizability and selection bias, while peer reviewers also SUPPORT, acknowledging limitations and praising the use of simulation to address small sample concerns.

Both address overall conclusions and significance (C127-C128, C134, C136). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, arguing strong claims are undermined by methodological limitations, while peer reviewers SUPPORT, affirming the study presents 'important findings' of 'significant interest' with conclusions 'mostly well supported by data.'

Minor overlap on relationship findings summary (C132). OpenEval includes this in UNCERTAIN evaluation questioning generalizability claims, while peer reviewers include it in SUPPORTED evaluation of the 18-month relationship finding.

Minor overlap on replicability claims (C133). OpenEval questions these claims as overstated given limitations, while peer reviewers include this in their overall SUPPORTED evaluation of the specification curve analysis.
